source_document.body:
CPC Fleet Solutions used to spend one to two months finding a single drop yard for its private fleets. Through Truck Parking Club’s Fleet Parking service, it secured seven yards for 47 power units and more than 120 trailers in two months, Truck Parking Club said in a Nov. 12 release.
For a fleet that hauls for shippers, yard space can decide whether a new lane happens at all. Truck Parking Club already lets fleets book five or more truck and trailer spaces as a single account . Its Fleet Parking team takes on the legwork: a dedicated specialist finds the yards, works with the property owners and puts every site on one account and one monthly invoice.
The search often starts when a shipper awards a new lane, said Reed Loustalot, Truck Parking Club’s chief marketing officer.
“If you get a new lane from a shipper and it requires drop trailers and there’s nowhere at their DC for them to store them, you’ve got to go find a piece of property,” Loustalot told FreightWaves. “It’s going to take you some time, and sales might be waiting on an okay that we can do the business.”
How CPC found yards before
Based in Chesterfield, Missouri, CPC Logistics was founded in 1973 . It runs private fleets for shippers across North America through CPC Fleet Solutions, according to the release.
Those fleets need domicile yards for specific clients and drop yards at relay points, said Nick Sablich, a regional manager at CPC Fleet Solutions. Finding each one fell to CPC managers, who looked at properties, negotiated and went “back and forth to legal, making sure all the red lines are met,” he said.
“To go find a yard the old way, it was taking at least a month or two months, even more,” he said in the release. “Having you guys as the liaison to talk to the property owners saved me about 10 years of my life.”
What the Fleet Parking specialist does
Working with Truck Parking Club’s Fleet Parking Team, a fleet tells its dedicated specialist where it needs space, how many trucks and trailers it has to park and for how long. It also lists what the site must have, such as cameras, gated access or fencing. The specialist then searches more than 7,600 locations, plus a broader network of private, fleet-only sites, to find the best, most efficient location for those requirements. If nothing in the network fits, the team sources a new yard.
A fleet “can send us an address and be like, ‘Hey, we need 25 spaces within five miles of here, and they need these amenities,'” Loustalot said. In his example, that meant a fence, gate, lights and 24/7 access.
Every yard sits under one Truck Parking Club account, and each location can carry the fleet’s cost code. That removes the site visits, cold calls, checks and one-off legal agreements a fleet would otherwise handle for every new yard, Loustalot said.
“Freight moves faster than real estate,” Kaleb Knipp, vice president of Fleet Parking at Truck Parking Club, said in the release. “A new lane or a lost yard should not take two months to solve.”
CPC tests yards before committing
The release says CPC started with three yards in August and moved all three to one-year agreements in September. It now has yards in five states, with more under review.
Sablich called trying a site first one of the best things CPC could do. A location “might look great on the map, but it might not work,” he said.
“Down towards Atlanta, the traffic is real tough in those areas. Or if you’re up in the mountains, the grade that you have to go on up the mountain, it could slow down hours of service , how many gate houses they have to go through,” he said. “Sometimes if you try it to see how it works first, you get a better plan of operationally how you can make it work.”
Overflow space for shippers
The yards also cover lanes where CPC has nowhere to leave trailers.
“It comes down to drop rights,” Sablich said. “If we start up a new lane and we don’t have the drop rights and we need to move trailers somewhere, we have that option now to do that.”
When a client’s own lot fills up, CPC can have Truck Parking Club book an overflow yard for a month, he said. Peak season brings another use: shippers doing inventory hold on to trailers and need more before they can unload. Being able to offer staging options in those areas has “expanded our portfolio to help out with our clients,” Sablich said.
“Our time is money, and we have saved thousands of hours doing it this way,” he said.
Loustalot said Truck Parking Club plans to keep adding locations, with a focus on getting denser in high-demand markets. “Every single location we add is a new option for a fleet to service customers in new ways,” he said.
Why it matters: Dedicated and private fleet operators quoting new shipper lanes can line up drop yards without a months-long search and put manager time back on running the fleet.
